propositions.text: A drug patent holder can protect the patent under Patented Medicines Regulations starting when the Minister lists the patent on the register.
The listing date on the patent register is critical for protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that patent protection under the Regulations begins when the Minister lists the patent, and the listing date is critical.

propositions.text: Serono argues the Minister unreasonably delayed listing their patent, causing loss of rights.
Serono says the Minister's approach fails to respect statutory, regulatory, treaty obligations, and policies.
Serono asks to quash the Minister's decision and declare the patent listed as of the earlier date it should have been added.
Intervener Innovative Medicines Canada supports Serono's position.

paragraphs.summary: Serono alleges unreasonable delay and failure to respect obligations by the Minister, seeking to quash the decision; IMC supports Serono.

propositions.text: The Minister and Apotex argue the Minister's approach was reasonable and legally sound.
They ask to dismiss Serono's application for judicial review.
Intervener Canadian Generic Pharmaceutical Association supports the respondents.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister and Apotex argue the Minister's approach was reasonable and ask to dismiss Serono's application; CGPA supports them.

propositions.text: The sole issue is whether the Minister's decision was unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the sole issue as whether the Minister's decision was unreasonable.

propositions.text: The Minister's decision on the listing date was not unreasonable under the Regulations and case law.
The Minister adds patents to the register only when eligible, not sooner or later.
Serono's application for judicial review must be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Minister's decision reasonable and dismisses Serono's application for judicial review.

propositions.text: The Regulations refer to drug patent holders as 'first persons' and generic drug companies as 'second persons.'

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Regulations define 'first persons' as patent holders and 'second persons' as generic companies.

propositions.text: The Minister must maintain a patent register and decide if patents meet eligibility requirements before listing.
Eligibility requires the patent to relate to an approved medicine, formulation, dosage form, or use (s 4(2)).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the Minister's obligation to maintain a register and eligibility criteria for listing patents.

propositions.text: Once a patent is listed, second persons are prohibited from entering the market except under strict conditions (s 7(1)).
Second persons must address listed patents before marketing generics (ss 5(1) and 5(4)).
This system is called the 'frozen register' because it fixes patents second persons must address at a point in time.
Second persons can address patents by accepting non-entry, consent, or alleging invalidity or non-infringement (s 5(2.1)).

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the 'frozen register' system restricting second persons' market entry and requiring them to address listed patents.

propositions.text: If a second person alleges invalidity or non-infringement, it must serve a Notice of Allegation on the first person (s 5(3)).
The first person can bring an infringement action, which bars market entry for 24 months (s 7(1)(d)).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the Notice of Allegation process and infringement action that bars market entry for 24 months.

propositions.text: Serono filed Canadian Patent No 3,087,419 in December 2005, granted March 7, 2023, titled 'Cladribine Regimen for Treating Multiple Sclerosis.'

paragraphs.summary: The court states Serono filed and was granted the '419 patent for treating multiple sclerosis.

propositions.text: Serono submitted patent lists for the '419 patent on March 16, 2023, against MAVENCLAD drug.
Health Canada screened the lists March 17 and preliminarily analyzed eligibility March 21, 2023.
OSIP informed Serono on March 23, 2023, that the patent lists were added to the register as of that date.

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts Serono's submission and the Minister's addition of the patent lists to the register on March 23, 2023.

propositions.text: Apotex filed its generic submission for MAVENCLAD on March 22, 2023, before the patent was listed.
Because the patent was not yet listed, Apotex appeared not to have to address the '419 patent.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Apotex filed a generic submission before the patent was listed, so it seemed not to have to address the patent.

propositions.text: Serono asked OSIP on April 20, 2023, to reconsider the listing date to March 16, 2023, the submission date.
If the earlier date applied, Apotex would have had to address the patent on March 22, 2023.

paragraphs.summary: Serono requested reconsideration to list the patent as of March 16, so Apotex would have to address it on March 22.

propositions.text: OSIP informed Serono the Minister maintained the listing date of March 23, 2023, the eligibility decision date.

paragraphs.summary: OSIP informed Serono the Minister kept the listing date as March 23, 2023.

propositions.text: The Regulations distinguish between submitting a patent list and adding a patent to the register.
The Minister must add only patents meeting eligibility requirements to the register (s 3(2)).
A patent is eligible if it claims an approved medicinal ingredient, formulation, dosage form, or use (s 4(2)).

paragraphs.summary: The Minister found the Regulations distinguish submission from addition, and only eligible patents are added to the register.

propositions.text: Section 5(1) requires second persons to address submitted patent lists.
Section 5(2.1) requires NOA statements to be directed at patents on the register.
These provisions reinforce the distinction between submission and addition to the register.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister found s 5(1) and s 5(2.1) reinforce the distinction between patent list submission and addition to the register.

propositions.text: The Minister rejected Serono's argument that eligible patent lists should be added on submission date.
Second persons do not have to address patents added on or after their submission date (ss 5(1),(4)).
These provisions confirm the distinction between submission and addition to the register.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister rejected Serono's argument and cited provisions confirming the distinction between submission and addition dates.

propositions.text: The 2006 Regulatory Impact Assessment Statement confirms second persons must address patents actually added to the register.
Health Canada's Guidance Document supports that the correct date is the eligibility decision date, not submission date.
These documents support the Minister's conclusion on the correct listing date.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister cited the 2006 RIAS and Guidance Document supporting that patents are listed on eligibility decision date, not submission date.

propositions.text: The Regulations aim to balance patent enforcement with timely generic entry.
Requiring second persons to address patents added after their submission would upset this balance.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister found the Regulations balance patent enforcement and generic entry, which would be upset by requiring addressing patents added after submission.

propositions.text: Case law (Eli Lilly) supports that second persons must address patents found eligible and added to the register, not merely filed.
Justice Barnes rejected Lilly's argument that the Minister had discretion to list on submission date.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister found case law supports addressing only patents added to the register, rejecting discretion to list on submission date.

propositions.text: Serono describes the Regulations as a race between first and second persons regarding patent listing and drug submissions.
Serono filed patent lists on March 16, 2023; Apotex filed drug submission on March 22, 2023.
Serono attributes the one-week delay in patent addition to the register to the Minister.

paragraphs.summary: Serono says the Regulations create a race between first and second persons, filed patents and drug submissions on specific dates, and blames the Minister for a one-week delay in patent listing.

propositions.text: Minister's decision to add patent a week after submission was unreasonable; no discretion to delay under s 3(2).
Delay risks depriving first persons of patent rights, contrary to Regulations' intent.
Minister failed to consider argument of arbitrary delay and did not explain delay between March 16 and 23.

paragraphs.summary: Serono argues the Minister's delay was unreasonable, risks patent rights, and lacked explanation or consideration of arbitrary delay.

propositions.text: Serono relies on s 5(1) wording requiring second persons to address patents submitted by first persons.
Critical date is patent submission date, not addition date; other interpretation ignores 'submitted' meaning.

paragraphs.summary: Serono argues second persons must address patents submitted before their drug submission, focusing on submission date, not addition date.

propositions.text: Eli Lilly case is distinguishable; Lilly's patent was initially ineligible and later found eligible.
Serono differs by arguing Minister should review eligibility immediately, not a week later.

paragraphs.summary: Serono distinguishes Eli Lilly case and argues for immediate eligibility review, unlike Lilly's delayed eligibility.

propositions.text: Serono compares to Abbott case where patent was relisted retroactively after wrongful delisting.
Serono argues patent should be added as of submission date or at least March 21, 2023, when eligibility review completed.
No justification for two-day delay between review and eligibility decision.

paragraphs.summary: Serono compares to Abbott case and argues patent should be added as of submission or eligibility review date, with no delay justification.

propositions.text: Listing delays violate Canada's obligations under CUSMA requiring fair balancing of first and second persons' interests.
Minister's SOP states patents must be examined 'immediately' if possible.

paragraphs.summary: Serono argues listing delays violate CUSMA obligations and Minister's SOP requires immediate patent examination.

propositions.text: IMC agrees patent should have been added on March 21, 2023, eligibility date; two-day delay penalized Serono.

paragraphs.summary: IMC concurs patent should be added on eligibility date; Minister's delay penalized Serono.

propositions.text: IMC argues second persons should address patents submitted before their drug submission to protect eligible patents.
Regulations balance public interest in innovation and patent value by granting first persons rights and 24-month stay.
Minister must interpret Regulations reasonably to respect significant interests of first and second persons.

paragraphs.summary: IMC argues second persons must address patents submitted before their drug submission to protect innovation and patent rights.

propositions.text: IMC argues addressing patents added after drug submission would not prejudice second persons who can update submissions.

paragraphs.summary: IMC argues second persons can update submissions to address patents added after their drug submission without prejudice.

propositions.text: Disagrees with Serono and IMC's characterization; Minister's decision was not unreasonable given Regulations, case law, and facts.

paragraphs.summary: Court disagrees with Serono and IMC, finds Minister's decision not unreasonable in context.

propositions.text: Agrees with Serono and IMC on Regulations' basic purposes and balance between first and second persons.
Disagrees that Regulations require immediate patent addition or addressing patents not yet added.
Minister has no discretion to delay adding patents but exercises discretion on eligibility determination.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees on Regulations' purpose but disagrees that immediate addition or addressing unadded patents is required; Minister has discretion on eligibility.

propositions.text: Interpreting Regulations provisions in isolation is unreasonable.
Subsection 3(2) requires maintaining register of patents submitted for addition, suggesting second persons address submitted patents.
Subsection 5(1) requires second persons to address patents submitted by first persons, reinforcing above interpretation if read alone.
But Regulations say more beyond these provisions, so isolated reading is incomplete.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds isolated reading of subsections 3(2) and 5(1) suggests addressing submitted patents, but Regulations say more, so isolated reading is unreasonable.

propositions.text: Regulations require register to contain patents found eligible by Minister, not immediately upon submission.
Minister must add patents meeting eligibility requirements and refuse ineligible ones per subsections 3(2)(a) and (b).

paragraphs.summary: Court finds register contains only patents found eligible by Minister, who must add eligible and refuse ineligible patents.

propositions.text: Second persons must address patents on register at time of their submission per s 5(2.1).
Second persons need not address patents added after their submission per s 5(4)(a).

paragraphs.summary: Court finds second persons address patents on register at submission time and need not address patents added later.

propositions.text: Reading Regulations as Serono and IMC urge is unreasonable as it overlooks other provisions providing context.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes Serono and IMC's narrow reading is unreasonable as it ignores other contextual provisions.

propositions.text: Minister reasonably relied on 2006 RIAS supporting interpretation that only patents found eligible and added must be addressed.
Generic manufacturers address patents on register at filing date; patents added later do not require addressing.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Minister reasonably relied on 2006 RIAS that only patents found eligible and added must be addressed by generics at filing date.

propositions.text: Minister reasonably relied on Guidance Document stating patents added only after eligibility review and second persons address only added patents.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Minister reasonably relied on Guidance Document confirming patents added after eligibility review and second persons address only added patents.

propositions.text: Minister's interpretation supported by Eli Lilly case where patent listing date was eligibility date, not submission date.
Lilly submitted patent list in Nov 2006; patent found ineligible then eligible in Nov 2007; Minister refused backdating.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Minister's interpretation supported by Eli Lilly case where patent listing date was eligibility date, not submission date.

propositions.text: Justice Barnes found Minister's decision correct applying correctness standard, calling Lilly's argument tenuous and self-serving.
Justice Barnes interpreted provisions as listing patents contemporaneously with eligibility determination.
Second persons need not address patents added after their submission per ss 5(4).

paragraphs.summary: Justice Barnes found Minister's decision correct, interpreting listing contemporaneous with eligibility and second persons need not address later patents.

propositions.text: Justice Barnes noted burden of delay falls on first persons as legislative choice.
Lilly's urged interpretation would cause problems by requiring addressing ineligible patents.

paragraphs.summary: Justice Barnes noted delay burden on first persons is legislative choice and Lilly's interpretation would cause problems addressing ineligible patents.

propositions.text: Serono argues Eli Lilly is distinguishable because it involved a patent first found ineligible, then eligible
Difference in Eli Lilly is irrelevant; Justice Barnes' interpretation of Regulations is binding and not erroneous

paragraphs.summary: Serono argues Eli Lilly differs due to patent eligibility sequence; court finds this difference irrelevant and upholds Justice Barnes' interpretation.

propositions.text: Cases relied on by Serono are distinguishable and do not assist its position

paragraphs.summary: Court finds cases Serono relies on are distinguishable and unhelpful to its argument.

propositions.text: In Abbott, Minister delisted patent after regulatory amendments but patent was found eligible for listing
Justice Simpson ordered patent added to register as of delisting date, not original submission or listing date
Abbott does not assist in interpreting Regulations here nor advance Serono's position

paragraphs.summary: Abbott case involved delisting and relisting patent; Justice Simpson ordered listing from delisting date; court finds Abbott unhelpful to Serono.

propositions.text: In Èquiterre, Minister had statutory duty to start special reviews of banned pest control products
Minister unreasonably delayed initiating some special reviews; obligation arose immediately upon awareness

paragraphs.summary: In Èquiterre, Minister had immediate duty to start special reviews of banned products; delay was unreasonable per Justice Phelan.

propositions.text: Serono argues Minister must immediately review and add eligible patents to register
Justice Phelan required review within reasonable time, not immediate action; reasonable time undefined
Health Canada screened Serono's patent day after submission; eligibility review completed four days later
Minister added patent to register same day eligibility was determined, March 23, 2023; no delay found

paragraphs.summary: Serono argues for immediate listing; court finds reasonable time standard applies; Health Canada acted promptly with no delay.

propositions.text: Minister's interpretation of Regulations is not unreasonable
Regulations require Minister to add patents meeting requirements and refuse those that do not (ss 3(2)(a),(b))
Minister must determine eligibility of submitted patents before adding to register (s 4(2))
Addition to register is not automatic; requires eligibility review of patent claims

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Minister's interpretation reasonable; Regulations require eligibility determination before adding patents to register.

propositions.text: Second person must address patents submitted, reviewed, and added to register (ss 5(1),(2.1))
Second person need not address patents submitted but not yet added or added after second person's drug submission (s 5(4)(a))

paragraphs.summary: Court explains second person's obligations apply only to patents added to register before their drug submission date.

propositions.text: Minister properly added Serono's patent on eligibility determination date, March 23, 2023
Apotex's drug submission on March 22, 2023 preceded patent addition; Apotex had no obligation to address patent

paragraphs.summary: Court finds patent was properly added after Apotex's submission; Apotex had no duty to address it.

propositions.text: Minister's decision to list Serono's patent on eligibility determination date was not unreasonable
Application for judicial review is dismissed

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes Minister's listing decision was reasonable and dismisses judicial review application.

propositions.text: Parties agree costs follow middle of Column III of Tariff B with no costs to interveners
Parties may make submissions on costs within 10 days of decision issuance
Judgment dismisses application; costs awarded to respondents per Tariff B; submissions on costs allowed

paragraphs.summary: Court orders dismissal with costs per Tariff B; parties may submit on costs within 10 days.
